Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

vignette: Case Vignette: Mr. Kim Mr. Kim, a 50-year-old South Eastern Asian man and musician, has been struggling with the lingering effects of his traumatic experience after being stalked over several months. The harassment was relentless, marked by constant surveillance and threatening messages that culminated in an attack during one of his performances at a local venue. Although he managed to escape, the event left him feeling vulnerable and exposed. What frightened Mr. Kim most was not just the physical threat but also the profound sense of betrayal and inadequacy that lingered afterward. He had come to believe that he was weak and that the institutions meant to protect him—police and security personnel—had let him down. This belief in his own weakness fueled a pervasive fear that left him vigilant and hypervigilant, especially at night when the darkness made it harder for him to feel safe. The trauma had fractured his memories of the event. When he tried to recall details, there were large gaps he simply could not fill in. However, when fragments of the memory did surface, they came without warning and with a startling vividness that felt completely real, assaulting all his senses at once. These sudden pieces of memory often triggered intense anxiety and fear, leading him to avoid unfamiliar places where he felt even more vulnerable. His sense of emotional numbness was another consequence of this trauma. Mr. Kim described feeling dead inside, as if the attack had taken a part of him with it. This profound disconnection from his emotions made it difficult for him to feel anything meaningful or connect with others on an emotional level. He watched other people closely, especially those he encountered in public spaces, looking for any signs that they might harm him. The more he felt emotionally numb and weak, the more vigilant he became, creating a cycle where his negative appraisals intensified his fear of danger. This constant state of threat monitoring led to increased anxiety, which in turn triggered more intrusive memories. The sudden pieces of memory would often arise when he was least prepared, making it hard for him to trust any environment as safe. His occupation as a musician had become particularly challenging. He avoided performing at unfamiliar venues and struggled with rehearsals that required traveling to new places. This led to strained relationships with his bandmates and colleagues, who found his behavior increasingly difficult to understand. The cumulative effect of these changes in his professional life was significant; he began to question his ability to continue working as a musician. The memory gaps and intrusive sensory reliving made it impossible for him to find peace even when physically safe. Nighttime intensified this sense of vulnerability, making sleep elusive and fragmented. Mr. Kim found himself constantly scanning the environment, unable to relax or let down his guard. What finally brought Mr. Kim to seek help was a combination of these overwhelming symptoms and the realization that he could no longer continue his career as a musician without support. He was most afraid of being completely powerless against future threats but also hoped for a way to reclaim some sense of safety and emotional connection. Mr. Kim’s current state is one of profound distress, with his negative appraisals reinforcing his threat vigilance and memory intrusions in a self-perpetuating cycle. His journey towards healing will require addressing these interconnected components to break the loop that has been tightening around him for months.
